extracted.intended_audience: literary students, critics, and creative writers interested in archetypal romance and quest narratives
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing or composing romance (quest) narratives with attention to archetypal structure, motifs, characterization, and symbolic/ritual associations described in Frye's archetypal criticism. Useful for critics seeking formal principles and writers shaping quest-driven romances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance as wish-fulfilment dream and social projection
rubrics_metrics.description: The romance is nearest of all literary forms to the wish-fulfilment dream; ruling social or intellectual classes project their ideals in romance (chivalric, aristocratic, bourgeois, revolutionary), while a perennial 'proletarian' element in romance keeps it returning in new incarnations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romance is marked by persistent nostalgia and a search for an imaginative golden age; expect social-class inflection in the ideals portrayed. Examples: chivalric romance (Middle Ages), bourgeois romance (since 18th century), revolutionary romance (contemporary Russia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential element: adventure; sequential/processional plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential element of plot in romance is adventure; romance is naturally sequential and processional, better known from fiction than drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romances often consist of a sequence of minor adventures leading up to a major, climacteric adventure (the quest). At its most naive, a static central character endures endless episodic adventures; in literary form the sequence is usually organized toward a announced climactic quest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest structure: three main stages (agon, pathos, anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete form of the romance is the successful quest, which has three main stages: the perilous journey and preliminary minor adventures; the crucial struggle (often a battle with death); and the exaltation of the hero (recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frye uses Greek terms: agon (conflict), pathos (death-struggle), anagnorisis (recognition). Many romances also employ the three-day rhythm (death, disappearance, revival) and motifs of 'third son' or third attempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic hero vs antagonist and cyclical/nature imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: A quest involving conflict assumes protagonist (hero) and antagonist (enemy). As romance approaches myth, the hero acquires semi-divine attributes and the enemy demonic ones; the hero is associated with spring/dawn/order/fertility/youth and the enemy with winter/darkness/sterility/old age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect cyclical imagery (seasonal, solar) and natural oppositions assimilated to moral poles. Critics may map such images to solar myths, but Frye warns this is often a literary device of displacement rather than literal descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth vs romance distinction: divine vs human hero; canonical status
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth differs from romance in that mythal heroes are divine and occupy a canonical position, whereas romance heroes are human; both belong to mythopoeic literature, but myth carries greater metaphorical identification and reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical myths (e.g., Adam and Eve) act as metaphorical keys to displacements found in romance; legends and folktales may nonetheless contain concentrated mythical meaning without canonical expurgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dragon-killing as central quest motif
rubrics_metrics.description: The dragon-killing theme (e.g., St. George, Perseus) exemplifies the central form of quest-romance: land ruled by an impotent old king is ravaged by a monster; victims are offered, the hero kills the dragon, marries the daughter, and succeeds to the kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ritual analogies: the dragon often symbolizes sterility of the land or the king's impotence. Expect motifs of sacrifice, deliverance, and succession; Christian analogues portray the hero as Messiah and the rescued bride as Church.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underworld/labyrinth motif: descent, death, and rebirth
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes commonly enter a dark labyrinthine underworld or the belly of a monster, undergo perilous navigation, and return with redeemed victims or treasure; this movement connects to death and cyclic rebirth themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Jonah, Theseus, Tom Sawyer, Beowulf; functions as structural principle across sophistication levels. May appear as literal caves, periods of past time, or symbolic inner journeys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold aspect of quest-myth: agon, pathos, sparagmos, anagnorisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the three-stage quest, Frye identifies four distinguishable aspects: agon (conflict), pathos (death), sparagmos (disappearance/tearing to pieces), and anagnorisis (reappearance/recognition leading to renewal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sparagmos can include ritual division of the hero's body (Eucharistic overtones) and distribution of parts in the natural world (Osiris/Orpheus). The full sequence often ends in rebirth/resurrection symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards and costs of the quest: treasure, bride, wisdom, mutilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Secular quests commonly reward treasure (representing ideal forms of wealth like power and wisdom) or a bride; prophetic sibyls and oracles inhabit lower worlds. Mutilation or handicap is often the price for unusual wisdom or power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Holy Grail (Eucharistic and fertility symbolism), bleeding lance, Hephaistos/Weyland, and sibyl-like prophetic figures. Treasure may symbolize fertility or potential life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic characterization: polarization and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization in romance tends to be polarized and simple: characters are either for or against the quest, idealized if supportive, caricatured if obstructive; subtlety and complexity are less favored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect moral opposites confronting each other (like chess pieces). Heroes and villains serve clear dialectical functions; irony plays little role in romance compared to other modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: White/black moral poles and archetypal helper figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'white' pieces strive for the quest (hero, lady, old wise man) and have counterparts in an 'old wise man' (Merlin, Prospero) and a sibylline wise mother who waits at home; black counterparts include evil magicians and 'terrible mother' witch-figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roles include mentors (old wise man), feminine quest patrons (lady/queen), and antagonists (Archimago, Duessa). The queen/wise female may function as bride or mother-figure with complex relations to the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-spirits / children of nature as morally neutral intensifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who elude moral antithesis (nymphs, half-wild daughter-figures, green men, wild boys) suggest spirits of nature: they are morally neutral, mysterious, and intensify the romantic mood while retreating when approached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Florimell, Hawthorne's Pearl, Wagner's Kundry, Kipling's Mowgli, Robin Hood. These figures can serve the hero (Friday/servant helpers) and are romantic analogues of comic buffoons or the architectus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic analogues to comic character types (four poles of characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance shows four poles of characterization analogous to comedy: hero vs enemy (eiron/alazon parallel), nature-spirits as buffoon/master-of-ceremonies, and other parallels to comic roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for equivalents of comic function: intensifiers of mood, ceremonial characters, and possible agroikos-type figures that highlight realistic aspects. This mapping helps classify romantic characters by function rather than realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism figures as safety-valves (fearful dwarf, Sancho Panza)
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance often includes a figure who voices fear or realistic concerns (dwarf with 'needments', Sancho Panza, jester Sir Dinadan) to localize realism without destroying the romantic mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characters permit moments of practical comment or fear; they can be framed as loyal or gallant to keep them within the romance's conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six isolatable phases of a romantic hero's life (cyclical sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance has six isolatable phases forming a cyclical sequence in the hero's life: (1) birth myth, (2) innocent youth, (3) normal quest, (4) maintenance of innocent world (analogous to comic final phase), plus further phases paralleling tragedy/comedy not fully enumerated here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phases map onto mythic/ritual cycles. The essay details phases 1–4 with examples (birth ark/flood; pastoral youth; quest; moral allegory/defense of innocence). Expect the remaining phases to complete the cycle toward social consolidation or comic closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birth-myth motifs: flood, ark, rescue, secret parentage
rubrics_metrics.description: The birth myth phase commonly involves a deluge/ark motif, infant placed in a chest/ark, rescue by animals, concealed paternity, and a false father figure who seeks the child's death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Perseus, Moses, Noah; stylistic associations include water/boat/reeds and images of the embryo in the womb. The motif links to future wealth/potential fertility and secret parentage tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent-youth motifs: pastoral Arcadia and sexual barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: The second phase is the innocent youth—an Arcadian, pastoral world (glades, brooks, moon) associated with chaste love and a sense of proximity to moral taboo; heraldic colors are green and gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect imagery of vanished youth and a dividing barrier (river/fire) between innocence and sexual contact, often signaling the impending fall into experience. Examples: Keats's Endymion, Rasselas, Purgatorio's garden of Eden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic/religious associations and sacraments in romance imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance imagery often fuses ritual and erotic symbolism: three-day rhythms, Eucharistic resonances (division and sharing of body), sacraments (water/tree of life), and color-symbolism (red/white = flesh/blood, bread/wine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spenser's St. George motif exemplifies red-and-white symbolism tied to sacraments and national allegory. Recognize ritual echoes (baptism, water of life) in the hero's trials and rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest motivations: Messianic deliverance vs secular rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Romances may present a Messianic hero who redeems society (religious deliverance), or secular quests that seek obvious rewards like treasure, power, a bride, or wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret whether the quest is typologically tied to biblical/mythic deliverance (Adam/Christ typology) or to secular themes (buried hoard, marriage). The symbolic meaning of rewards (wealth as fertility, bride as ambiguous maternal figure) should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarization of feminine figures: lady of duty vs lady of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance often polarizes female figures into a 'lady of duty' (virtuous bride/queen) and a 'lady of pleasure' (enticing damsel), sometimes resolved by reconciliation (mother-in-law motif) or left in enmity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect narrative tension between duty and pleasure (e.g., Psyche and Venus). Reconciliation themes are common; where absent, the older female tends toward the sinister (stepmother archetype).
